Based on the distortion contours presented in Figure 39, significant changes are observed once molten salt enters the tank after Day 27, and the filling process continues. As the salt inventory increases, the hydrostatic pressure it exerts causes the floor plates to slightly deflect downward toward the foundation. This 'flattening effect' exerted by the molten salt tends to cause radial expansion of the tank floor, thereby increasing stress near the perimeter. 33 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. The maximum and average von Mises stress in the tank floor and wall are presented in Figure 40. Both the maximum and average stress are higher in the floor due to the high restriction on this component's ability to expand and contract during preheating. Initially, the maximum stress in the floor relaxes to a value just above 250 MPa. The stress relaxes slowly until Day 25, then rises due to the increase in hydrostatic pressure exerted by a sufficiently high molten salt inventory (i.e., a level of 1 m) after day 27. Figure 40. Maximum and average von Mises stress evolution in the tank floor during 27 days of preheating followed by a few hours of tank filling. 34 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4 Final Remarks 4.1 Conclusions and Lessons Learned The behavior of commercial-scale molten salt thermal energy storage (TES) tanks for central receiver concentrating solar power (CSP) plants was initially modeled and analyzed as part of the DOE SETO- funded project, agreement DE-EE0038475—'Failure analysis of molten salt tanks for in-service CSP plants' Tasks 1 through 5. This foundational work involved formulating and validating a physics-based model in a Multiphysics simulation environment using typical plant operation conditions [4]. This report presents the analysis and findings from two subsequent tasks focusing on tank size and preheating. Key conclusions and lessons learned from this final phase of work are summarized below: - Results indicate that operational stress increases with tank diameter, supporting the engineering preference for fabricating smaller-diameter tanks to achieve lower stress levels. In addition to the tank diameter, additional benefits in terms of stress reduction can be achieved by using thicker floors as was presented in the previous report [4]. - The thermo-elastic-plastic FE method with shell elements, used to investigate two tank floors with diameters of 24 m and 32 m led to a peak von Mises stress of 596 MPa upon completion of all welds.
